Urban Economics is intended as a two-part course. Module 1 is 5258: Urban Economics I and Module 2 is 5259: Urban Economics II.Cities are the most productive, innovative, and unequal places humans have ever built. They also contain the vast majority of real estate wealth and opportunity. These module courses give students the economic tools to understand why. You will learn why cities exist, what drives their growth, and how to answer questions regarding major urban trends reshaping cities today using the core concepts of economics. How does the market value land and buildings, and what are the implications for development profitability, housing affordability, transit investment, and municipal fiscal health? How are cities adapting since the remote work revolution? Why does the housing crisis persist? How quickly will the market eliminate excess inventory in the office sector and what policy measures are required to speed this process?The Urban Economics I and II modules move through these questions in two arcs. The first module, 5258, builds foundations of microeconomic reasoning, urban growth and agglomeration, labor markets, land rent, and the spatial models that explain how value is distributed across cities. The second module, 5259, applies those frameworks to the policy challenges planners face most directly: housing markets and affordability, local public finance, transit economics, segregation and neighborhood opportunity, and climate vulnerability.5258: Urban Economics I assumes no prior economics background. Some sessions involve graphing and basic algebraic reasoning, but no calculus is required. It does assume that you care about cities and are willing to let economic reasoning complicate your intuitions about them. 5259: Urban Economics II assumes knowledge equivalent to that covered in 5258, Module 1.Students in the GSD Real Estate program are required to take 5258, Module 1. They are also required to take Module 2, 5260: Market Analysis for Real Estate Development and Investment. MRE students may choose to enroll concurrently in 5259: Urban Economics II as an elective. course_title: Science at the Frontier of Unsolved Medical Problems
description: We ask in this class how fundamental science, pathophysiological insights, and AI can be harnessed to understand disease and to design approaches to improve human health. We begin with an introduction to some areas where fundamental knowledge -- for example in genetics, immunology, and oncogenes -- have led to striking recent changes in therapy. We then focus on two areas where medicine has made less progress: disorders of the brain and failure of organ systems. As in Frontiers in Therapeutics, the prior version of this class, each session will begin with a lecture by an expert in the field.  This will then be followed by student-led discussions of papers relevant to the topic. Students will learn how to evaluate the relevance of fundamental science to seemingly intractable medical problems, as well as the credibility of proposed novel therapeutic opportunities.

course_title: The Translational Science of Stem Cells: Present and Future
description: Information about the biology of stem cells and their uses in understanding and treating diseases -- particularly those that cannot be studied adequately in non-human model systems -- has increased enormously in the last decade. In this seminar/lecture course, students will learn about transplanting functional human cells (such as pancreatic beta cells or dopaminergic neurons) derived from pluripotent cells to treat disease. They will also discover how to use these cells to model diseases, such as neurodegenerative and cardiovascular diseases, with the goal of identifying more effective, possibly patient-specific, therapeutics. Students will hear about treatments, including small molecules (conventional medicines), whose therapeutic actions can be attributed to the regulation of tissue-specific stem cells that reside in key adult tissues including the bone marrow and brain, but, interestingly, not including the heart or pancreas. Finally, they will be exposed to relatively new work that demonstrates the possibility of creating new cells from old by using genetic methods to swap cell identities. A typical type of question that we will debate is: When should Parkinson’s disease patients be treated with a drug to slow the death of neurons, with transplanted neurons made from pluripotent cells or with a viral vector that produces new neurons from existing glial cells in the brain? This course will highlight the theoretical, as well as the practical, aspects of drug development. How are therapies progressed from conception to patient (bench to bedside)? How can academic investigators commercialize research? Importantly, while this is a science course, not a health economics course, we intend to discuss ways of reducing drug costs. At the same time, we will introduce the new trend of treating rare (even N=1) genetic diseases and how this is or isn’t accommodated within our existing healthcare framework. We believe that students with different backgrounds (biology, chemistry, engineering, business) and at different levels (undergraduate, graduate) can benefit from taking the course and will help enrich the discussions by providing different perspectives on topics that we’ll cover. However, basic knowledge of cell and molecular biology will be needed to understand the course fully.

description: Nearly one in three residents of the United States lives close to the poverty line, and a growing number of people live in deep poverty, subsisting on less than $2 per day. This course examines the social world of poverty in the US today. It pays particular attention to the lived experiences of low-income people. It also examines the parallel sets of institutions low-income people must navigate—institutions that often perpetuate poverty, like low-wage jobs, systems of policing and surveillance, substandard schools and colleges, exploitative housing, and predatory financial services. The course places a heavy emphasis on firsthand experience and learning. We will have guest lectures from people whose work or life experiences relate to the course subject matter. Students will also complete several fieldwork assignments, doing things like observing eviction court, applying for food stamps, or interviewing someone making ends meet at a low-wage job.

What is society? What is the role of the individual in it? How can we change our societies? This course introduces students to the field of sociology. By surveying social theory as well as empirical studies, students acquire what C. Wright Mills calls the "sociological imagination": the ability to think beyond our personal lives and to connect the experiences of individuals with large social structures. We examine common-sense assumptions about culture, politics, history, and psychology, and empower students to replace them with evidence-based reasoning. This gateway course introduces students to the intellectual insights and analytical tools of Sociology across the subfields of race, class, gender, politics, violence, culture, and inequality. Students are trained to critically analyze the evidence and research methods used in sociological research, and to communicate sociological ideas powerfully and succinctly through effective policy writing. Whether you plan to become a doctor who understands the social determinants of health, an education expert seeking to improve US schools, a not-for-profit worker supporting community organization, or a corporate consultant looking to improve organizational efficiency, the foundational concepts and research practices of sociology will empower you to understand, analyze—and maybe even change—our social world.

course_title: Analytic Methods of Urban Planning: Quantitative [Module 2]
description: This course introduces students to quantitative analysis and research methods for urban planning. The course begins with an examination of how quantitative methods fit within the broader analytic landscape. It then exposes students to basic descriptive statistics (including measures of central tendency and dispersion), principles of statistical inference, and a wide variety of analytic methods and their practical application. By the end of the course, students will be comfortable with many analytic techniques relevant to urban planning and policy, including: z-tests, t-tests, ANOVA, chi square tests, correlation, and multivariate regression. On a broader level, students will gain the ability to understand and critically question the kinds of analyses and representations of quantitative data encountered in urban planning and allied disciplines.The aim of the course is to introduce students to key concepts and tools in quantitative analysis and research. Most importantly, however, the goal is to develop students’ intuition regarding data analysis and the application of statistical techniques. By the end of the course, students will be familiar with how common techniques of quantitative analysis can be applied to a wide variety of data. Students will also gain a sense of the strengths and weaknesses of quantitative data analysis and under what circumstances the tools learned in the class are best applied in practice. The course seeks to train technically competent, intellectually critical practitioners and scholars who are able to apply quantitative methods in a wide range of settings, and who are also aware of the wider analytic context into which these approaches fit. There is a focus throughout the course on epistemology and the ethics of claim-making. Over the course, students will deepen their understanding of how claims are made, how claims are connected to different forms of evidence, and what makes different kinds of claims credible.

course_title: From Cells to Tissues, in Sickness and in Health
description: Every cell is a part of a larger “community”, working together to enable tissue function. This course will explore the principles of building complex tissues from cells. How do cells know what tissues to make and when to make them? How do cells communicate with one another? What diseases can arise when these principles go awry? How can we build tissues in the lab? In addition to lectures, students will engage deeply in primary literature.

description: This course approaches families as social arrangements shaped by broader forces and as arenas in which we make choices about our lives. As such, we will consider how family forms and relationships reflect wider systems of gender, race, class, sexuality, and state policy, as well as how they provide sites of resistance to dominant social norms. We will focus on contemporary studies of key aspects of family, such as: partnering and marriage, diversity of family forms and chosen family, reproduction, childrearing, work–family arrangements, care work, and aging. Our goal is for students to develop tools to critically analyze contemporary debates about “the family” and reflect on their own assumptions about what families are and what they do. As a seminar, assessment will be based on close reading of assigned texts, participation in discussion, and development of a student-led project.

course_title: Analytic Methods of Urban Planning: Qualitative [Module 2]
description: How can planners develop a deep, systematic understanding of communities and places? This module explores the critical role of qualitative research in both planning practice and scholarship. Students will investigate how qualitative methods answer complex “why” and “how” questions, uncover different perspectives and lived experiences, illuminate local values, and help interpret unique, complex, and nuanced situations.Emphasizing hands-on learning, the course guides students through the process of designing qualitative research projects tailored to community and organizational contexts. A range of data collection and analysis methods will be covered, including artifact review, place observation and ethnography, interviewing, group engagement, and visual techniques for both interpreting and presenting data. Students will also learn to use conceptual frameworks to organize qualitative evidence into compelling outputs, such as diagrams, case studies, scenarios, evaluations, and assessments. Students will leverage weekly exercises as an opportunity to practice and refine these approaches.The course will equip students with practical qualitative research skills and critical analytical frameworks, laying a foundation for careers in urban planning and its related fields, where understanding people and place is essential for creating effective, equitable, and context-sensitive solutions.

course_title: The Materiality of Writing in the Ancient World: Sumerian, Cuneiform, and Beyond
description: Cuneiform, the world’s earliest writing system, was invented over 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia (ancient Iraq). It was originally used to write the Sumerian language, a language that continued to be written for over 3 millennia and produced a corpus of well over 100,000 preserved texts. The act of writing—a means of externalizing and visually representing language—has an inherent materiality to it, one that was new and innovative in the ancient world. In this class, we explore the relationship between the Sumerian language and the materiality of its writing, covering topics such as the invention and development of cuneiform; the material process of making a clay tablet; the use of Sumerian writing in conjunction with other media; and wider functions of cuneiform writing. Over the course of the semester, students learn enough Sumerian grammar and vocabulary to read simple Sumerian royal inscriptions from the original cuneiform. The class meets in the collections of the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East and provides students the opportunity to work directly with cuneiform objects.

This course serves as a transition between the survey nature of the sophomore tutorial and the independent senior thesis in Theater, Dance & Media at Harvard. We engage with methods and forms of theater, dance and media which may provide inspiration for your future artistic and scholarly work. Our strategy is to identify a number of contemporary and historical performances and performance archives and critically consider how they might influence your evolving identity as an artist working in live media, dance, and performance. We will delve deeply into genres of arts practices that could help you to imagine a way forward in your own work. In doing so, the goal is to advance your transition into a professional life in theater, dance, and media, and the identify your key concerns (both artistic and pragmatic) regarding a professional practice. Throughout the semester we will discuss how your personal goals and concerns intersect with political, social, and individual contemporary preoccupations in those fields.  This junior tutorial is designed to organize participants into a community of singular artist interlocutors who can also supportively engage with one another’s projects. You will develop methods to articulate your own intentions and impulses with great specificity, offer appropriate feedback for the stage of development for your peer’s projects, and acquire facility with terms of art in theater, dance & media.  Our semester is oriented to gaining autonomy and independence in relation to your interests. For the first seven weeks of the semester, we will read and explore a number of topics and ideas regarding the development of a sustainable arts practice, all the while, developing a specific set of questions pertinent to each class member’s interests in the concentration. At the end of the seven weeks, students will present (both in person and online) on a company or artist whose work you have been researching in depth (the options are outlined in week 7 of the syllabus). We then pivot to your topics brought up during the first half of the semester – in essence the class will be building and completing the syllabus for the last half of October and November and December, while discussing and workshopping the development of their thesis ideas.

course_title: Building Equitable Cities: Policy Tools for Housing and Community Development
description: This course explores how U.S. cities can foster more inclusive and equitable futures through housing, economic development, and place-based investment strategies. Grounded in racial and spatial inequality realities, students will examine how public policy, at the federal, state, and local levels, can be harnessed to build stronger, more just communities.Topics include affordable housing finance and production, equitable transit-oriented development, displacement and gentrification, neighborhood revitalization, climate resilience, and tools such as tax credits, public land use, and community development finance. The course critically assesses contemporary initiatives like Opportunity Zones and Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, focusing on whether they address or perpetuate systemic exclusion.A defining feature of this course is its applied, problem-solving orientation. Students will produce a short policy memo and collaborate on a term-long group project that proposes concrete, equity-driven strategies to address a housing or community development challenge in a specific U.S. city. Projects are grounded in real-world policy contexts and designed with the potential to inform public or nonprofit sector action.Ideal for students interested in urban policy, community development, affordable housing, or public leadership roles, the course centers the urgent work of building equitable cities - neighborhood by neighborhood, policy by policy.

description: This course analyzes what role the government plays and should play in a market economy, especially those policies that work through taxes and government spending. It covers topics such as tax and welfare policy, unemployment insurance, social security, environmental protection, and state and local policy. The course emphasizes recent empirical research on policy issues and will teach students how to conduct such studies.The first half of the course, taught by Professor Stantcheva, will cover the basic principles of public economics. These principles will be used to shed light on current questions and debates on tax policy, the provision of public goods, and social insurance.The second half of the course, taught by Professor Veuger, will highlight recent empirical research on business taxation, the regulatory state, political economy, and multilevel government. In this part of course we will also see how the theoretical and empirical approaches covered in the course can be and have been used to inform and assess the economic policy response to the COVID-19 crisis, in particular in the United States and Europe.

course_title: Why Innovations in Education Fail—and How They Can Succeed: From K to Gray
description: The world is experiencing an unprecedented rate of change thanks to technology. Education—schools, companies, systems—must adapt rapidly, but our current tools and structures are failing students and society. This course offers tested theories and frameworks grounded in real-world case studies to help you understand the current landscape and take an active role in reshaping education. Whether you are a (future) founder, a learning designer, a policymaker, an administrator, a teacher, an investor, or someone who simply wants to make a meaningful impact in education, this course will equip you to analyze different organizations/companies/systems and push for change at various levels of impact—from the system to the classroom. The theories we study will also explain why some innovations succeed while others fail. Each class, we learn about a theory, such as disruptive innovation, and ground it in the work of real organizations and education companies from around the world. Students will use these frameworks to understand system dynamics, identify opportunities for change, and design solutions that are both effective and sustainable. This course is essentially a flipped classroom model. Class sessions are fully interactive. Students will engage in case studies, group discussions, simulations, and active learning. They will teach core theories to one another and apply them collaboratively to real-world education problems. Many class sessions include visits (either in-person or virtually) from the individuals featured in the case studies. description: This course provides a broad introduction to surface transportation policy and practice in the United States in the 21st century, covering its development, current status and changes underway in transportation systems and policy at the local, state federal levels. Together we will explore how U.S. transportation policy has evolved and potential levers for changing the policies that shape how people access the places they want to go using motor vehicles, public transportation, passenger rail, micromobility, walking and biking. First we will examine the purposes of transportation and transportation policy and the tradeoffs and tensions among competing values and desired outcomes. Next, with the assistance of guest lecturers with both government and advocacy experience, we will cover the institutional, program delivery, and governance structures that shape policy and the financing methods that fund infrastructure projects. In the last part of the course, we will survey a series of current critical transportation policy debates, with students helping determine which topics to address.

course_title: Principles and Practice of Biochemical and Cell Based Assays in Drug Discovery
description: The overarching objective of this course is an introduction to the essential topics in biochemistry and cell biology relevant to assay design, drug discovery and therapeutic sciences. This foundational course combines lectures and lab-based training to provide students with fundamental knowledge emphasizing their application in assay development. Through hands-on laboratory sessions, participants will learn to translate theoretical concepts into practical skills, gaining experience in assay design, data analysis, and experimental planning. Additionally, students will receive comprehensive training in record-keeping and documentation of research using electronic laboratory notebooks. The curriculum comprehensively addresses key areas of contemporary drug discovery, including assay technologies, enzyme kinetics, biochemical principles, and receptor and ion channel pharmacology. This allows students to develop both biochemical and cell-based assays, allowing them to design rigorous experiments and interpret complex data effectively. By closely aligning practical training with core scientific concepts, this course prepares students thoroughly for advanced study and experimental work in their thesis laboratories.

course_title: Making the American City: Form and Society
description: To understand today’s urgent social, environmental, and development issues, Making the American City: Form and Society explores the history of American urban growth, planning, and design. By examining specific plans and places, it traces the growth and elaboration of major North American cities from the early European settlement to the present, with an emphasis on the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Through the study of plans, physical projects, and material conditions, the course investigates specific topics, such as the downtown; homes and housing; public parks and landscapes; planned communities and civic spaces; transportation systems; environmental threats and disasters; the provision of infrastructure; racial and ethnic settlement patterns; slums and ghettos; bohemias and art districts; urban renewal and revitalization; gentrification; and suburbia in all its diversity. The objective of the course is to use history to inform the thinking and practice of contemporary planners, policy makers, and designers. Through lectures, discussions, texts, and films, this course aims to impart a fundamental knowledge of the major events that have contributed to the form and character of modern American cities.
notes: Also offered by the Graduate School of Design as HIS-4488.  Please note, this is a jointly offered course hosted by another Harvard school and, accordingly, students must adhere to the academic and attendance policies of that school.

The course provides an introduction to the Sumerian language, a language isolate spoken in ancient Mesopotamia and probably the world’s first written language. Although several aspects of Sumerian remain debatable, students learn the fundamentals of the grammar and writing system as well as the most common cuneiform signs in a variety of lapidary and cursive contexts. Many of the texts that are covered are a variety of dedicatory inscriptions from the time of Gudea (ca. mid-twenty-second century BCE) and the subsequent Ur III dynasty (ca. twenty-first century BCE), but other genres and time periods are sampled as well. This study of the Sumerian language also includes some background on the culture and history of the Sumerians. Course to be taught by Dr. Anna Glenn.

This course provides foundational training in experimental design and data literacy tailored specifically for biomedical research. Students will systematically design experiments and learn methods to collect, organize, and analyze biomedical data. Emphasis is placed on practical, hands-on experience using statistical and data-management software tools. Through interactive lectures, discussion forums, group activities, and case studies, students will explore real-world scenarios and actively identify potential pitfalls, biases, and limitations inherent in biomedical research. By the end of the course, students will possess the critical thinking skills needed to design robust experiments, confidently select appropriate statistical methods, and accurately analyze and interpret experimental results. They will also recognize and mitigate common pitfalls, biases, and limitations, preparing them for effective biomedical research.

Mount Tremper: The Artifice and the Sublime - Landscape, Threshold, and Dwelling
description: This studio examines the Catskills as a landscape already dense with cultural, aesthetic, and ecological meaning. Its identity has been shaped by nineteenth century discourses of the sublime, the Hudson River School, and Transcendentalism. In the absence of European architectural antiquity, American artists like Thomas Cole transformed wilderness into a cultural monument, making mountains and forests vehicles for national identity, spirituality, and environmental consciousness. This lineage, articulated philosophically by Emerson and Thoreau who defined nature as the arena for American spirituality and personal autonomy, moves from overwhelming spectacle toward sustained attention. Landscape reveals itself not merely as scenery but as atmosphere, memory, deep time, and spiritual ground. Dwelling here is an ongoing dialogue with natural reclamation, a condition framed by Georg Simmel’s “The Ruin,” which locates aesthetic equilibrium in the balance between human artifice and entropy.At the center lies Tremper, an 182-acre site in the Catskills being developed as a mission driven sanctuary where art, ecology, and hospitality converge. The project is grounded in the conviction that community benefit and economic sustainability reinforce each other. Students will design a 35-room wellness retreat, expand an existing art center, and build a multipurpose ecology facility as interdependent typologies. Drawing on Japanese “town as hotel” models, the art center and hotel form a complementary pair. The hotel provides privacy and seclusion, while the art center delivers activation and cultural life, addressing rural hospitality’s chronic off-season emptiness. Ecology sits between them as a bridge, integrating culture, landscape, and human experience into a single system.The studio embraces total design, carrying interiors, furniture, and objects holistically with architecture. Students will design an integrated object of encounter, such as a piece of furniture, handrail, window detail, or lighting fixture, where the smallest detail carries the same conceptual weight as the largest gesture, echoing Wagner’s Gesamtkunstwerk at site scale.Readings in aesthetic theory, phenomenology, and Eastern spatial traditions, including the tea ceremony, engawa, ma, and borrowed scenery, frame the interrogation of landscape and dwelling. The studio questions whether communion with nature emerges through tolerated disharmony, drawing on the “savage” as aesthetic imperfection, Boym’s ruinophilia, and Shinohara's anti-functional spaces.Two field trips anchor this inquiry. A site visit to the Catskills grounds the studio in atmospheric and cultural reality. A trip to Porto, Portugal, examines works by Távora, Siza, and Souto de Moura, offering critical perspective on how regional traditions are interpreted through modern architectural language. Evaluation considers conceptual depth, design rigor, clarity of expression, and coherence of the final proposal. Active participation in desk critiques, pin-ups, and field trips is required.This studio is supported by the Kenzō Tange Visiting Chair in Architecture and Urban Design.

course_title: Rebuild: The Politics of Design - Case Studies in Transformational Urban Redevelopment
description: What does it mean for an urban redevelopment project to be transformational? Only a select group of projects earn this distinction, those that achieve lasting change through inclusive community engagement, sustainable design, innovative policy and financing, and a thoughtful balance between the historical and the new. These projects demonstrate how the built environment can serve as a catalyst for equity, resilience, and long-term transformation. ReBuild offers a unique, case-based approach to learning from 4–6 real-world examples of transformational urban redevelopment across American and international cities. Through interactive analysis and discussion, students will unpack the complex interplay of public policy, design, financing, and community priorities that shape these projects. The case studies include large-scale public and private investments that aim to significantly revitalize their built and natural environments, incorporating infrastructure upgrades, adaptive reuse, new construction, and public space creation. Each case provides students the opportunity to simulate real-world roles, evaluate competing priorities, and propose solutions grounded in practice and theory. Students will: Gain insights into the social, economic, and environmental forces at play in transformational redevelopment efforts. Build practical skills in urban analysis, stakeholder engagement, decision-making under complexity, and integrated design thinking. Strengthen their ability to generate context-specific insights that inform more equitable and effective planning and development strategies. Case studies are the core of this course’s pedagogy. Each case presents a richly detailed, real-world scenario with complex problems, stakeholder tensions, and multiple decision points. Students will explore these cases through: Collaborative discussion and facilitated debate. Problem-solving workshops simulating real-world planning and design challenges. Role-playing and scenario analysis to understand competing perspectives. This active learning model moves beyond passive lecture-based instruction. It immerses students in the decision-making process, helping them develop critical thinking, persuasive communication, and the confidence to shape real urban futures. By the end of the course, students will not only understand how transformative redevelopment happens—they will be prepared to lead it.

description: Although market and other mechanisms of private ordering determine much about how people use and develop land, externalities and collective-action problems require coordination and regulation. The legal system—through legislation, administration, and litigation—shapes the built and natural environment, bringing public values into the management of private property.  Zoning ordinances, for example, set use and density limits as well as processes for development approval, influencing the geography of economic and demographic diversity, while environmental laws seek to limit pollution, regulate ecosystems, and respond to climate change. This course provides students with working knowledge of important land use and related environmental laws as well as the institutions that create, implement, and review them. The course also considers what distinguishes law from other fields, as well as the roles that planners, designers, policymakers, real estate professionals, and the public play in land use and environmental law.  Through class discussions, the course engages with primary sources, such as zoning ordinances and judicial opinions, as well as secondary material, and requires no legal background. The course involves an exercise in proposing reforms to a component of a local land use law and a final exam.
notes: Also offered by the Graduate School of Design as SES-05206. Permission of the instructor required.  Please note, this is a jointly offered course hosted by another Harvard school and, accordingly, students must adhere to the academic and attendance policies of that school.

description: Students will research the extraction of stone, the production of masonry units, and their tectonic language. Medieval cryptographic languages and diagrams will be studied as a means to invent new cryptographic languages for tectonic and construction operations. Students will develop a historical understanding of defensible and sacred architecture to inform new strategies in masonry, security, and sacred programming. Quarry visits will include open-air granite operations in Barre, Vermont, and underground marble mining in Danby, Vermont. Instruction from specialists in masonry, diplomacy, defense, disaster planning, history, and engineering will inform student work, strategies, and research.The studio asks how architecture can respond to 21stcentury existential threats - AI, biowarfare, pandemics, climate change, weaponized technology - that erode democratic institutions and existing security alliances. Since masonry has historically served both defensive and sacred programs, can a new coupling of the sacred and the defensible produce spiritual and diplomatic forms of collective security for a world where old alliances no longer hold, and can new rituals unite an increasingly atomized society?Each student will design new masonry systems and cast units that generate space, structure, and light through the innovation of program and site. Working individually, each student designs a place of spiritual contemplation that also offers collective security and defense. Individual projects are sited in a quarry and other locations on earth or in outer space that host security programs and architectural interventions. Students will collectively design a proto-urban landscape that incorporates each of their individual projects.Students are evaluated on the rigor of their research into material, symbolic, historical, and technical histories. They are also evaluated on the craft, theory, conceptual rigor, and structural logic of their designed and cast masonry projects, including fabrication quality and casting / finishing technique. Evaluation also considers the conceptual and innovative strength of the sacred / defense programmatic coupling and spatial manifestation in the final intervention, along with how effectively individual projects are collectively integrated into a new proto-urban condition. Communication through drawing and model making is evaluated for clarity and inventiveness.Students will develop hands-on fabrication skills (casting, finishing, and detailing of masonry units) and grounding in masonry techniques - conceptual clarity and technical literacy directly transferable to material driven practice. More broadly, the studio explores existential conditions through programmatic innovations in diplomacy, security, and spirituality, translating them into architectural form with refined tectonic details. Individual works are integrated into a coherent collective urban condition, inventing a new civic order with public rituals meant to unite. Architecture is understood as both a social science and a spatial material art form.

course_title: Reenvisioning the Longest, Wickedest Street in America: Colfax Avenue, Colorado
description: There is an avenue in the western United States that cuts across the entire spectrum of urban and rural conditions. At 26 miles, it is the longest continuous commercial street in the United States. It runs from the town of Golden at the base of the Rocky Mountains to the town of Strasburg, just out of view from their peaks in the rural great plains. It crosses through four counties, eight townships, and one major metropolis. Playboy magazine once called it “the longest, wickedest street in America.” Colfax Avenue collapses the American condition into a single line, slicing through both the wealthiest (80238) and most economically challenged (80204) zip codes in Colorado. Largely built out in the mid-twentieth century and then subsequently left fallow, its stock of commercial buildings, bars, night clubs, motels, restaurants, and gas stations are remarkably well preserved. Colfax is a microcosm of the American landscape: mundane, industrious, worn, garish, polished, and dulled.Colfax’s contested history, its troubled present, and its wildly diverse mix of contexts makes it a compressed and syncopated analogy for the array of conditions that are pervasive across the urban, suburban, mountainous, and rural conditions of the entire country. Evaluating the mundane and vernacular conditions found across it reveals an analogy of contemporary life. When taken in its entirety, it exposes an array of conditions rendered self-similar by the flatness of the street itself. This studio will make a deep examination of this context’s many idiosyncrasies and particularities in order to build a lexicon of intensely local urban form and construction typologies. We will use this catalog to build a reflective language of architecture that comments and builds upon this context to generate architectural novelty.Each student, taking a section of Colfax Avenue, will develop a project type reflective of that section and projective of its architecture. Each student will mine their corridor of Colfax Avenue to devise their own project brief within the confines of one or some combination of the following four programs: Motel, Theatre, Casino, Strip Mall. Students will be asked to analyze, stretch, destroy, and reconstruct the models and physical typologies that these ‘programs’ represent to the boundaries of their own individually conceived polemic. Students will likewise be asked to examine a single specific construction method common to the region to pull on it for local particularities that can be likewise extrapolated.Students will work individually on projects that engage in the production of digitally produced and highly graphic work represented in printed media both in flatness and in the form of physical models. There will be a midterm and final assessment along with two periodic assessments at the quarter-marks.

description: Las Pozas in Xilitla, Mexico, is one of the most extraordinary architectural landscapes of the twentieth century — a surrealist garden interlaced within the Sierra Huasteca jungle, imagined and built by the English eccentric Edward James beginning in 1962, after a frost killed the thousands of orchids he had spent years collecting. What replaced them was stranger and more durable: a proliferation of concrete follies, stairways to nowhere, columns without ceilings, arches framing only sky, and the jungle that surrounds it all. A radical conception of the type that would have made Piranesi proud.Xilitla offers a new way of thinking about architecture and its relationship to nature. As opposed to the more defensive posture of fighting against nature that has characterized much of the last century, simply keeping it at bay, we are here confronted with an extraordinarily unique context that offers a symbiotic relation between the two. Las Pozas offers an architecture becoming part of larger processes of transformations — oxidation, weathering, biological growth, and erosion. Moss, rust, and wear are not accidents to be prevented; they are anticipated agents in the design and life of its structures. Its meaning depends on the tropical cloud forest, the liquidity of the atmosphere, the density of vegetation, the steep topography, the waterfalls and pools, the constant cycle of growth and decay. Architecture here is inseparable from the ecological forces acting upon it.Here we understand how nature speaks. And this context, too, presents an equally rare opportunity to understand how architecture is made. The structures of Las Pozas were cast using handcrafted timber formwork, fabricated by local carpenters with a precision and inventiveness that the finished concrete only partially reveals. These molds are, in a precise sense, the hidden architecture behind the architecture. And they survive. Dispersed across Xilitla in bars, workshops, sheds, private homes, and storage yards. Architecture rarely turns its gaze toward its own instruments of production — the scaffolding, the formwork, the jig, the mold. These are treated as temporary, subordinate, expendable.This studio begins with two questions. How can architecture exhibit the process of its own making? And how can it do so within an environment where building and nature are not opposed but choreographed?After a research trip to Mexico, visiting Mexico City, Las Pozas, and the site itself, the studio proposes designing a new cultural institution for Xilitla: a Museum of Formwork. The program will encompass galleries for original formworks, today scattered seemingly at random across the town, new conservation and restoration facilities, research and archive spaces, educational workshops for local craftsmen, and artist and researcher residencies. Equally important will be the landscape and gathering spaces that engage the town beyond the boundaries of Las Pozas itself. Students will be challenged to rethink the museum typology from first principles — to imagine architecture that reveals how it is made, that anticipates how it will change, and that treats process, in both senses, as content.

course_title: Metropolitan Transformation in Lima, Peru. Designing through Systems, Space, Governance and Value
description: Metropolitan regions are shaped by the interaction of infrastructure, governance, investment, environmental systems, mobility networks, public space, and evolving patterns of everyday life. Yet urban interventions are often conceived through fragmented approaches, where urban systems are planned in isolation, separating mobility from land use, public space from economic development, and spatial design from governance and implementation. This studio explores how metropolitan transformation can emerge through integrated approaches that connect systems, spatial design, governance, and value creation.Lima provides a unique context for this exploration. As a coastal desert metropolis framed by the Pacific Ocean and the Andes, and home to more than 11 million people, Lima is Peru’s political, economic, cultural (with both millennia-old and colonial heritage), and gastronomic capital, as well as one of Latin America’s leading tourism destinations. The studio focuses on Lima’s evolving metropolitan centralities, where new mobility infrastructure, changing patterns of work and investment, the emergence of mixed-use urban environments, and growing ambitions for high-quality public spaces, sustainability, and urban livability are reshaping the metropolitan core. At the same time, these opportunities unfold within a broader metropolitan context marked by chronic traffic congestion, spatial fragmentation, and unequal access to urban opportunities, raising important questions about how growth, investment, and design can contribute to more connected, resilient, productive, and inclusive metropolitan futures.Working across the disciplines of urban design and planning, students will explore metropolitan transformation through interconnected systems, including mobility and connectivity systems, public realm and urban activation systems, metropolitan centralities and urban value systems, ecological and landscape systems, innovation and economic development systems, and human experience systems. Through readings spanning fiction, non-fiction, and urban scholarship, lectures, discussions, mapping, precedent analysis, guest speakers, stakeholder engagement, and field observations, students will develop proposals that integrate design thinking with governance and implementation strategies across multiple urban scales.Students will work in pairs to produce analytical maps, systems diagrams, design proposals, physical and/or digital models, governance and implementation strategies, and an integrated vision for metropolitan transformation. Final projects will demonstrate how integrated urban interventions can contribute to long-term metropolitan transformation while generating spatial, environmental, social, institutional, and economic values.Student work will be evaluated on the rigor of research and analysis, the originality and quality of design proposals, the integration of systems thinking across scales, the ability to connect design with governance and implementation, the clarity of communication, and active participation throughout the semester.The studio is intended primarily for students in Urban Design and Urban Planning and welcomes students from Landscape Architecture, and related disciplines interested in metropolitan transformation, systems thinking, and interdisciplinary approaches to shaping cities.

course_title: Biospheric Urbanism - Case Study 5: Brussels, Belgium
description: Ambition and MethodologyCities are facing the accelerating effects of the climate crisis. Extreme heat, prolonged drought, and flash floods place unprecedented pressure on urban environments. The studio aims to be both pragmatic and visionary, developing concrete interventions while imagining how cities must evolve under increasingly severe climatic conditions.The Biospheric Urbanism studios explore the built environment as the interface between an uncertain meteorology and an underestimated geology. Each edition studies one city, building research across different climates. After New York City, Paris, Athens and Los Angeles, the Fall 2026 studio turns to Brussels.The studio is organized in three acts. First, working in groups, students will construct a climatic cartography of Brussels, revealing a mosaic of microclimates. By mapping heat, shade, wind, water, soil, vegetation, flood vulnerability, and patterns of occupation, they will identify areas of climatic urgency and their causes. Second, working individually, students will formulate strategies for selected sites and climatic challenges. Third, they will develop these strategies into spatial proposals and test their performance under different warming scenarios of 2, 3, 4 and 5 degrees Celsius.Case Study #5: BrusselsBrussels is vulnerable to rising temperatures because of its dense urban fabric, sealed surfaces, uneven tree cover and social inequalities. These conditions produce marked differences in heat exposure and thermal comfort. The covering and canalization of the river Senne in the nineteenth century largely removed water from the public realm, raising the question of how water can again become climatic infrastructure.Site Visit and PartnershipsStudents will travel to Brussels to investigate selected sites and to meet city representatives and local actors to understand local challenges and ambitions. The City of Brussels has expressed strong interest in the studio. At the end of the semester, the students will present their proposals to the city and explore the possibility of constructing on-site prototypes to test selected ideas.The studio will collaborate closely with Transsolar, an international climate engineering firm, which will introduce the principles of outdoor thermal comfort. Through workshops and desk critiques, students will integrate climatic analysis and performance evaluation into their designs.This studio is supported by the LUMA Landscape and Ecology Research Series.

course_title: Diversions: Minor Public Works of the Continental Divide
description: This option studio explores public works of water infrastructure—local and territorial, intimate and extensive—in the landscapes lying below the Continental Divide in Colorado. Over the course of the twentieth century, massive complexes of tunnels, pipes, and reservoirs ruptured regional geology for agriculture and urbanization, estranging ecosystems from atmospheric and ecological cycles. These mega-diversions are large in size but limited in scope. Against this context of altered regional hydrology, this studio seeks other states and behaviors of water that are less responsive to big, brittle infrastructure—not only runoff and creekflow, but also vapor, steam, ice, and slush. We will speculate on minor public works for new forms of physical encounter with the landscape, new programmatic possibilities of the interpretive center, and close-range, attentive modes of visual storytelling. Three coexistent and alternative kinds of public “diversions” structure the studio’s approach:Diversion 1: Recreation. Major and minor public waterworks are crisscrossed by recreational infrastructure—hot springs, hiking trails, ski resorts—drawing millions of residents and visitors annually. How will the effects of a dramatically changing climate (e.g., altered snowpack and streamflow) alter the relationships between these infrastructures? Students will design new thresholds, broadly at the scale of human experience, that anticipate and choreograph these transitions.Diversion 2: Managed Concealment. The landscapes of the Continental Divide are strewn with artifacts that attempt to translate the invisible conditions of the immediate environment (interpretive signage, visitor centers, etc.). These artifacts operate within the tradition of the landscape picturesque, diverting attention from evidence of human intervention, negative externalities, or banal functional adjacencies—such as parking lots and comfort stations. Students will design alternative forms of interpretation through landscapes and structures that stage new encounters between unsettled human and nonhuman worlds.Diversion 3: Divertissement. Twentieth-century images of this region were made strategically for distant consumption. The scenic photograph and the park brochure—which often captured the landscape in panoramic views—perpetuated the idea of this land as wild and vacant, redirecting attention away from embedded forms of indigenous habitation, mineral extraction, and phenomena that were then suited poorly to the camera. Students will explore producing short videos as site research: slow-moving images that demand close, sustained attention and serve no explicit promotional or economic agenda.We will travel to Colorado, visiting sites of infrastructure, recreation, and design (such as the Herbert Bayer Institute). Guest lecturers will offer guidance on hydrology, videomaking, and regional issues of design and ecology. Our trip will include visits to unpaved, relatively undeveloped landscapes. Also note that we will be at high elevations (+/- 5000 feet or 1700m above sea level) on exposed sites that may experience rapidly changing weather. Students will work independently, though participation in group workshops is integral to studio pedagogy; pairings will be considered upon discussion with the instructor. The studio’s output will include measured design drawings, small study models, renderings, and short videos.This studio is supported by the Koji Yanai Innovative Infrastructure Initiative Fund and the LUMA Landscape and Ecology Research Series.

course_title: Fall Dance Production Studio: Contact Improvisation
description: TDM Production Studios consist of a 4-credit course that meets weekly led by TDM Faculty and a full production process led by a professional Director or Choreographer which culminates in the public performance of an original work. This fall’s Production Studio will focus on Contact Improvisation, one of the most influential contemporary dance practices today which attracts and inspires dancers and non-dancers all over the world. Developed in the early 1970s, contact improvisation explores how two or more people move closely together through space, playing with physical forces such as momentum, gravity, and inertia.The course component, taught by dance scholar Laura Quinton, will delve into the history, theories, political, social, and practical applications of this global art form. We will also examine what it means to make a professional dance production, meeting with our choreographer, musicians, and designers to hear their insights into the creative process.The production component will be led by professional choreographer Stephanie Turner. In weekly rehearsals leading to a weekend of professionally produced performances, students will collaborate with Prof. Turner to create a new dance work rooted in contact improvisation, developing their individual artistic voices while building a shared movement language. What does it mean to fall, fly, rebound, and dance together in a turbulent world? And what might contact improvisation reveal about the value of human touch, physical expression, and live performance in our digital age? In the spirit of contact improvisation, all movers – seasoned or first-time – are welcome.
notes: TDM production studios (TDM 90AR/BR/CR/DR) frame and involve participation in Theater, Dance & Media’s professionally directed and designed productions. Additional evening rehearsals throughout the semester and final performances at the end of the semester are required; more details and schedule are on the Canvas course page.  All are welcome, no prior dance/movement background required.  Participation is limited to students involved with the production, either as performers or as members of the production team. Students who wish to be part of the production team should contact Artistic Producer James Stanley, jamesstanley@fas.harvard.edu.  This course satisfies the “Production Studio" requirement for TDM concentrators.

course_title: City in a City: Designing Downtown LA's Second Renaissance
description: Downtown Los Angeles (DTLA) is emblematic of contemporary urban design’s complexity and opportunity. How can an existing district be redesigned, adapted, and developed for today and tomorrow?Amid an expanse of dingbat apartments and strip malls, downtown Los Angeles is a paradox: a dense icon for a city it largely does not resemble. Yet DTLA is where the city gathers, celebrates, and drives economic development, with offices, hotels, schools, museums, dining, and roughly 90,000 residents drawn there over the past generation. The pandemic shifted everything and never fully stopped: office oversupply left real estate vulnerable, and declining public health and safety have made downtown less inviting as reasons to return grow.Acting as a single urban design team, the studio focuses on urban production at a moment when physical change faces social, political, and financial headwinds, requiring treating what we design and how we make it happen as one problem. City in a City asks what DTLA could become right now, in a few years, and across a generation, addressing five interlocking conditions: office vacancy and adaptive reuse, public realm quality, public health and safety, new construction, and connectivity.Proposals will be full spatial propositions: a building, a landscape, a street, an interior, or a specific product that increases attraction and interconnectivity in the district. Proposals reckon honestly with why conditions persist and what improvement costs in financial, political, and social capital. They should also be visionary, demonstrating how tomorrow’s downtown can be more attractive than today’s.The studio runs in two phases. Site investigation features mapping and policy research ahead of a visit to Los Angeles. Students pitch initial interventions, then test them in the field by meeting directly with business improvement districts, policymakers, community organizations, residents, business coalitions, designers, and developers, and by observing how DTLA's districts behave across conditions.Back in Cambridge, students develop full spatial proposals individually or in teams, depending on the scale of the intervention. Each proposal stands on its own, while aggregating into a unified strategic plan for the district. Feedback from studio partners continues through the semester, culminating in a final review and a public-facing report shared with the city and community.Each design proposal is developed to a high level of visual and conceptual articulation. Work is judged on three legs of urban production: design (a clear vision and form for the intervention), strategy (a near- and long-term plan for advancing it), and mechanism (how it is initiated, financed, and sustained). Given real capital scarcity, students must address market logic directly. This doesn't mean maximizing financial return but rather justifying the intervention’s cost in terms of social, cultural, and environmental gains. The studio is solution-oriented, and proposals are judged on what they can build, not on how well they describe the problem.Open to students in Urban Design, Architecture, Landscape Architecture, and Urban Planning. Given the studio's site-based, design-driven pace, students should be prepared to work with a high degree of agency, spatial command, and creative judgment from the outset.This studio is supported by the Los Angeles Headquarters Association, Building Owners and Managers Association Greater Los Angeles, the DTLA Alliance, and the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies.

This course will provide exposure to the diagnosis and pre- and post-operative care of the cardiac surgical patient, with direct involvement in patient care. course_title: Housing as an Ecology of Care: From Blank Type to Dwelling
description: This studio explores housing as an ecology of care, a framework that understands architecture as a relational practice embedded in networks of interdependence among people, species, systems, and time. In this view, a multi-story residential building is a place to live as well as to heal, connect, and coexist—a dwelling for human and nonhuman life.We will apply this lens to the transformation of an existing department store, the GALERIA Berlin Hermannplatz, an example of a building type that has shaped city centers in Europe and North America for over a century but which now faces obsolescence in the e-commerce era. The department store is the archetypal blank type: its facade bears no relationship to its interior, its depth exceeds what any habitable program can tolerate, and its spaces are organized around the display and movement of goods rather than people. Working within these constraints, we will approach the conversion of this blank type through five overlapping domains of care:Historical care preserves and reinterprets the building’s embedded history while avoiding the carbon cost of demolition. Integrating extant features such as atriums, escalators, and elevator and stair cores allows past labor and use to inform future dwellings.Planetary care explores how the deep, column-free floor plate that makes housing difficult can be opened to support human and non-human life, becoming an interior garden, light well, inhabited courtyard, or green roof.Social care asks how the store's spatial generosity—its wide corridors, open floors, and open ground-level—can be reworked to form an architecture of collective life that is also deeply connected to nonhuman life. Students will choose between two paths that express this differently: Living Together proposes collective ownership and shared domestic infrastructure; Living with Nature pursues social housing organized around intimate access to planted terraces, courtyards, and indoor gardens. Both paths assume the building belongs to its residents and to the city.Temporal care asks whether the building's capacity for interior change, designed for seasonal display and tenant fit-out, can be redirected to accommodate the evolving needs of residents and communities.Bodily care asks how spaces will feel when inhabited—the quality of light, the acoustic conditions, the tactile properties of materials—and how we can restore what the blank type suppressed.The department store is approximately 30,000 square meters. Working within the existing building, your proposal will house 300–500 residents, depending on ownership model and design path.Students will work individually throughout the semester. Philip Denny, as Teaching Associate, will be part of the teaching team. The studio will meet weekly on Thursdays and Fridays with Farshid Moussavi and Philip Denny in residence on alternate weeks. Professor Hanif Kara will collaborate with the studio during weeks 1 and 2 to address adaptive reuse.There is no planned studio travel, however, students will discuss their work with Berlin-based architects and experts. A virtual tour of the site and urban context information will be provided. Students are encouraged to enroll in the Housing Matters seminar, which provides helpful background and concepts for housing design.

course_title: Infrastructure Urbanism: Building Common Grounds across the Border – Between Hong Kong and Shenzhen
description: Ecological Backdrop: Blue-Green InfrastructureShenzhen and Hong Kong share a common blue-green ecological foundation along the Shenzhen River: one river, connected mountain ranges, and rolling hills. These primitive infrastructures underpin human settlements, providing the stage for daily life and economic activities.Urbanization: Hong Kong vs. ShenzhenGeopolitics have shaped two contrasting urbanization trajectories.South of the Shenzhen River, Hong Kong—since its colonial founding in 1841—developed a compact, high-density core on Hong Kong Island and Kowloon, expanding northward via rail-served new towns. Despite 185 years of urbanization and 70 years of modernization, Hong Kong retains 76% of its statutory non-development land, particularly in the north. The Northern Metropolis initiative now seeks cross-border integration with Shenzhen.North of the river, Shenzhen—since its Special Economic Zone establishment in 1980—leveraged geopolitical advantages, land economy, and high-tech industries to transform from a 30,000-person fishing village into a 20-million-person mega-city in just 45 years, achieving 100% urbanization. As land supply dwindles and the property market cools, Shenzhen is seeking industrial and spatial synergy with Hong Kong.Infrastructure-in-Between: River, Border, and IdentityThe 37 km Shenzhen River serves as a natural administrative boundary and former political divide. Since the reform era, it has become a composite infrastructure of land ports, cross-border bridges, rail lines, and flood control systems, supporting daily cross-border flows.The northern bank is fully urbanized with residential, commercial, and logistics functions. The southern New Territories side retains rural villages, farmland, fishponds, brownfields, and Hakka settlements—creating a sharp urban-rural contrast rare in the Greater Bay Area.With the Northern Metropolis and Hetao Cooperation Zone underway, both cities aim to transcend dual boundaries—rural/urban and administrative—while addressing flood control and ecological constraints. Re-examining cross-border systems and infrastructure capacity is key to the Shenzhen River’s future.The Imbalanced Spatial Development – Shenzhen Time Shenzhen’s rapid urbanization is undoubtedly a double-edged sword. While bringing economic and demographic dividends, the excessive pace of spatial development and population growth has led to severe land shortages. The rapid population increase has strained public infrastructure and supporting systems, creating significant imbalances. Issues such as energy and water shortages, along with an overtaxed environmental capacity, directly impact the quality of public life and the city’s sustainable future. The rapid development along the northern bank of the Shenzhen River epitomizes these challenges.This studio focuses on a 6km² area between Wenjindu and Liantang ports, with the 0.6 km² Luofang Water Treatment Plant and Luofang Village as the design site. This urban-edge district has undergone continuous renewal—village demolition and infrastructure redevelopment. With Hong Kong planning new town developments to the south, Shenzhen faces different challenges in urban renewal and industrial strategy. A studio trip to Hong Kong will take place in October. The studio will not be traveling to Shenzhen.

course_title: From Rust to Must: Reimagining McKeesport
description: For a century, Western Pennsylvania was called the Steel Capital of the world, pulsating year-round, day and night, with the production of steel for rail, bridges, ships, and buildings. As a bookend to Pittsburgh, McKeesport stood out in the Monongahela Valley as an urban hub. Downtown McKeesport had the tallest buildings outside Pittsburgh, busy streets, streetcars, the fancy stores, parades, and great parks. Then, seemingly overnight, industry stopped cold. Beginning in the 1970’s, competitive steel manufactured in Japan, South Korea, and other countries slowed down the demand for US-produced steel. US Companies were reluctant to modernize, inducing obsolescence. Higher costs of labor, energy and transportation accelerated the decline. By the 1990’s many mills in the Mon Valley had substantially scaled back production or altogether shut down—in some cases, without prior warning to the workforce. Thousands of people were left jobless, hollowing out communities and leaving hulking blast furnaces dark and silent. Pittsburgh rebounded. McKeesport did not. Two-thirds of its population was lost, and what was once a bustling downtown is run down and half empty. An effort is underway to reenvision the city’s downtown, tapping McKeesport most valuable asset: pride of place and community resilience. Another key asset is geographical: the downtown adjoins two rivers, the Monongahela and the Youghiogheny, the latter offering rare unincumbered access to the waterfront. National trends pointing to the affordability and benefits of small town living also portend a brighter future.Students will study the city’s past and current conditions, and over the course of the semester answer a fundamental question: Amid rapidly changing lifestyles and tectonic shifts in the global and national economies, how can McKeesport tap such trends and become a must place to live, work, and play? The focus of such question will be the city’s downtown.The studio will progress in three phases: 1) Historical understanding; 2) Imagining possible futures; and 3) Developing site-specific plans and designs. The first two phases will stretch through to the midterm review, leaving four to five weeks to develop individual plans and designs. Evaluation of the work will be based on research thoroughness; creativity in imagining possible futures (informed by relevant case studies); and communications skills, graphic and verbal, in answering the question above. The identification of specific sites, blocks, districts or neighborhoods for individual work will be determined following a site visit.The work plan will enable student to dream big—as big as the individuals who created the Mon Valley steel industry did one hundred fifty years ago—based on an understanding about how progress impacts cities, society at large, and the planet.This studio is supported by the Koji Yanai Innovative Infrastructure Initiative Fund.

course_title: Regenerative Adaptation: Harnessing Abundance in The Hydraulic Landscape of Kurobe
description: This studio aims to project a sustainable future for Kurobe, Japan, where the delicate balance among nature, industry, land, and the economy will be challenged by anticipated physical and social changes of great magnitude. Landscape architecture is the agent and medium of this projection for the future.The current stable land use of the Kurobe River alluvial fan owes much to the flood control and water supply projects carried out since the turn of the 20th century, especially the construction of upstream dams and a continuous protective embankment alongside the braided Kurobe River system within the alluvial fan. At the same time, constructing a mechanized, artesian irrigation network of canals and farmland consolidation across most of the area led to substantial growth in rice paddy cultivation. Combined with flood control measures, the hydrological structure of the alluvial fan has transformed significantly throughout the 20th century.In the meantime, from the mid-1950s, large-scale manufacturing businesses (YKK and YKKAP) that use non-ferrous metals as raw materials have established operations here, taking advantage of the alluvial fan’s abundant groundwater resources and stable electric power supply. Such efforts have helped drive the local economy and improve the livelihoods of Kurobe’s working population.However, practices of water use for agricultural development and industrial production have not been considered jointly or holistically, and as a result, these initiatives have drawn no particularly meaningful interaction despite the prosperity they owe to the same alluvial fan. The climate crisis requires us to think about an alternative, sustainable future for Kurobe, especially given the overutilized groundwater resource, extreme power demand, declining population, and the dynamics of the current industry that will be affected. The abundance of water resources, once treated as a danger (i.e., flood control) and then as an unlimited asset (i.e., industrial and agricultural establishment), must be reexamined holistically to allow for water, industry, and civic life in this region to become much more intertwined and nourish each other mutually.The studio will travel to Japan during the GSD’s preferred travel week. We will, first, spend two full days in Kyoto, the city that has flourished thanks to such abundant water resources of Kyoto Basin, to learn its hydraulic culture and to see how Kurobe can learn from the city. Then we will move to Kurobe to perform field research and acquire local knowledge. Thoughts and ideas will be tested and developed through various lectures and workshops during the semester, including the topics of Japanese rural landscape, traditional and contemporary Japanese landscape language, environmental engineering, and model making. The students enrolled in this studio are strongly encouraged to take the discussion-based seminar, “Designers of Mountain and Water: Alternative Landscapes for a Changing Climate (PRO-7453),” to gain a more fundamental understanding of the vicissitudes and unrealized potential of Japanese landscape architecture.This studio is supported by the Kyoto Protocol Studio and Research Fund.

For decades, architecture has pursued performance through optimization: more efficient, more precise, more controlled. This model relies on complex systems operating under stable conditions. As climate uncertainty and resource scarcity transform the environments in which buildings operate, this paradigm reveals its limits. Buildings optimized for stability often prove the least capable of accommodating change.The studio proposes robustness as a new understanding of architectural performance. It asks how performance might be redefined—not as the maximization of efficiency, but as the capacity to absorb uncertainty. Robustness privileges redundancy over precision, repair over replacement, and adaptability over permanence.Corporate office buildings provide a critical ground on which to test this shift. Built at an unprecedented scale and increasingly challenged by declining occupancy, they are among the building types most exposed to premature obsolescence. They depend on intensive mechanical systems and continuous maintenance, making them vulnerable to climate change and rising operating costs.The studio investigates how new climatic artifacts within existing buildings can challenge conventional approaches to adaptive reuse. Rather than programmatic change, proposals emerge from the interaction between climate, context, and low-tech climate systems.Brussels, home to the European Commission, contains 12.5 million m² of office space for 1.2 million inhabitants—one of Europe’s highest office-space-per-capita ratios. The studio trip will combine an in-depth understanding of the case study with meetings and discussions involving the various actors engaged in the transformation of these buildings. Much of this stock now faces premature obsolescence, while its ongoing transformation has typically relied on energy- and resource-intensive renovations.Guided by an economy of means, the studio will instead explore selective, resource-conscious approaches. Drawing on Layers of Change, we will read the building anatomically, assessing each component by its lifespan and adaptive potential. Prioritizing in situ reuse, we will repurpose existing components into new climatic artefacts.Rather than transforming the whole building, the studio will identify where limited interventions can produce the greatest architectural and climatic impact. We will develop climatic prototypes as architectural interventions evaluated through digital modeling and CGI imagery.Ultimately, the question is architectural: how does shift in value—from optimized objects to robust artifacts—reframe our understanding of new ways of living?This studio is supported by the John Portman Visiting Chair in Architecture.

AQUA INCOGNITA VI: Resilience Under New Climate Regimes in Valencia, Spain
description: The Aqua Incognita studio series follows research by design pedagogy to envision resilience in water-stressed territories. Focusing on the metropolitan region of Valencia, Spain, Aqua Incognita VI addresses the increasing fluidity between prolonged droughts and catastrophic DANA floods that in October 2024 took a heavy toll on human life, the environment, and infrastructure. How do we break free from this Sisyphean destructive cycle? Can the flood be transformed into an opportunity for socio-ecological regeneration?This summer, Valencia is entering a decisive new phase of post-DANA recovery. The Valencia Regional government has announced an international competition for the masterplan of the Metropolitan Floodable Parks System, a 1,500-hectare blue-green infrastructure extending along the Turia River and the Poyo and Saleta ravines. Conceived as one of Europe's most ambitious territorial regeneration projects, the initiative seeks to transform flood-prone landscapes into a continuous network of public open spaces capable of reducing flood risk while restoring ecological systems and strengthening metropolitan connectivity.Rather than treating this competition as a fixed framework, the studio will critically engage with its ambitions, exploring complementary design strategies and alternative futures for the Horta Sud.Horta Sud is the territory most severely impacted during the 2024 catastrophic floods along the Poyo Ravine. Separated from Valencia by the 1969 Turia River flood-control channel, the Horta Sud municipalities have evolved into an urban continuum, embedded within the Horta and the Albufera. The Horta, a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System (GIAHS) by UN FAO, is a millennium-old agroecological landscape sustained by a still-functioning network of gravity-fed acequias introduced during the Islamic period. The Albufera–Spain’s largest freshwater lagoon with RAMSAR protection–sits within the Parc Natural de l’Albufera. This cultural landscape, featuring traditional barracas, alquerías, and molinos, is collectively managed through irrigator communities and the Tribunal de las Aguas, Spain’s oldest water court–also with UNESCO recognition.Building on previous work, students will investigate how design can transform episodic flood events into long-term spatial, ecological, and material opportunities—supporting soil regeneration, wetland restoration, enhancing water quality, and new forms of housing and earthen construction techniques. Through this lens, the studio advances a hydro-social and ecological material framework, where water and earth are understood as interdependent cycles shaping the territory and not enemies to defend against.Working across scales—from watershed to settlement to lagoon—students will produce critical cartographies, engage with local actors, professors, and experts during our trip to Valencia, and develop site-specific design proposals. These proposals will aim to reduce flood risk while enhancing hydrological performance and the continuation of historical water and material cultures.This studio is supported by the Koji Yanai Innovative Infrastructure Initiative Fund and the LUMA Landscape and Ecology Research Series.

description: This advanced clinical clerkship offers students the rare opportunity to participate in the diagnosis, counseling, and management of complex fetal conditions that may require surgical intervention. Students will become integral members of a multidisciplinary care team including fellows, genetic counselors, nurses, maternal-fetal medicine specialists, neonatologists, and fetal surgeons gaining exposure to the full continuum of fetal and maternal care.What makes this experience unique is the dual nature of our patients: the fetus, or in many cases multiple fetuses, as the primary patient(s), the care givers, and the surrounding family as central partners in care. Unlike most specialties, students will confront the challenge of caring for a patient who cannot be directly examined history and physical examination cannot be performed on the fetus. Instead, students will learn to rely on advanced imaging, diagnostic testing, and collaborative interpretation to guide clinical decision-making. This integration of highly specialized maternal-fetal care with family-centered counseling provides a distinctive and invaluable learning experience.Clerkship activities include comprehensive patient evaluations, participation in prenatal consultations, and operative room experience in fetal surgeries. Students will also join structured educational activities, such as fetal intervention lectures, morbidity and mortality conferences, multidisciplinary case series reviews, and journal clubs. Surgical exposure may include procedures twin–twin transfusion syndrome, open spina bifida repair, chest and bladder drain placements and other complex fetal anomalies.
